PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

# Prop. 37 offers $25 billion to homebuyers to help with a down payment. Here's the catch
Proposition 37 on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households.
For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state's existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages.
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov.
Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.

# LA Voter Guide: Everything You Need To Know
## From the vote centers open right now to the races impacting the community — here's your voter guide for the city of Los Angeles.
### Statewide Propositions
#### Proposition 37
Proposition 37, which qualified for the ballot as an initiative statute, would authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to back a loan program to help middle-income earners enter the housing market.
Specifically, the proposed programs would provide loans of up to 17% of a home's purchase price to help buyers with the standard 20% down payment.
They would have to repay the loan to private lenders as with a standard mortgage payment.
The program would be open to buyers earning up to twice the area's median income.

Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface.
It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes.
Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home.
A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans.
When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk.
That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.

# PROP 37: The Middle-Class Homeownership Bond Initiative
###### Quick Facts
- **Official ballot title:** “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes.
Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general).
The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
- **Measure’s own name:** California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
- **Type:** Initiated state statute.
It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code.
It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
- **A vote YES means:** The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
- **A vote NO means:** No such program is created.
CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
- **Sponsor/proponent:** Robert M.
(Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition.
The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.

Designed to expand housing access, Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion state bond program providing eligible middle-income homebuyers with fixed-rate second mortgages covering up to 17% toward the purchase of newly constructed homes.

###### Vote Yes on Prop 37
Designed to expand housing access, Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion state bond program providing eligible middle-income homebuyers with fixed-rate second mortgages covering up to 17% toward the purchase of newly constructed homes.
...
In his Sept. 21 *Los Angeles Times* column, George Skelton argues that Proposition 37 is a straightforward, taxpayer-free way to help middle-income Californians achieve homeownership by addressing one of the biggest barriers to buying a home: the down payment.
Skelton points out that the $25 billion in revenue bonds would be repaid by participating homebuyers through their mortgages, rather than through taxpayer dollars or the state’s general fund.
Under the proposal, eligible California residents could put down as little as 3% on a newly constructed, owner-occupied home and finance the remaining 17% through a second mortgage.
Skelton also notes that the program would help expand the state’s housing supply and create construction jobs, while a recent Public Policy Institute of California poll found strong voter support for the measure.

This bond measure is strange, novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns.
Confused?

Prop.
37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments.
The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome.
That covers much of the typical 20% down payment.

Roughly 90% of all California renters.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

#### Proposition 37
Proposition 37, which qualified for the ballot as an initiative statute, would authorize up to $25 billion in bonds to back a loan program to help middle-income earners enter the housing market.
Specifically, the proposed programs would provide loans of up to 17% of a home's purchase price to help buyers with the standard 20% down payment.

The program would be open to buyers earning up to twice the area's median income.

Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.

Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. The Legislative Analyst lists exactly this—whether the program increases construction and homebuying—as an open question. That uncertainty is the heart of the trade-off.
Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].
The assistance is tied to newly built homes and paired with a builder option, so the design at least aims at expanding supply rather than only subsidizing demand [1, Sec. 51515.02].
The program lowers the down-payment barrier, the largest single obstacle for many first-time buyers, by covering up to 17 percent of the price [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)].
It carries real consumer protections. The loans must be fixed-rate, origination fees are capped, prepayment penalties are barred, and lenders face agency-set consumer rules [1, Sec. 51515.04].
The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?
If the loan pool underperforms, who actually bears the loss, and could the state face pressure to step in despite the no-liability language?
Does a ceiling of 200 percent of the area median income target the households with the greatest need or does it spread the subsidy to higher earners in costly counties?
How much of the subsidy reaches buyers as lower costs, and how much is captured by builders and sellers through higher new-home prices?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
This measure promises help for middle-class buyers at no cost to taxpayers. That is true only if borrowers repay $25 billion in bonds in full. Ask who is left holding the loss if they do not and whether a state agency running a program this large could really stand aside.
A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a new home only improves affordability if it also gets more homes built. Ask whether this measure will add enough new supply to keep from simply bidding up the price of the homes it covers.

Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted more than 900,000 signatures and qualified with over 600,000 valid signatures, above the 546,651 required for an initiated statute. It qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)

1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?

Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted more than 900,000 signatures and qualified with over 600,000 valid signatures, above the 546,651 required for an initiated statute. It qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.

The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].

6. Open questions

Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?

LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. The Legislative Analyst lists exactly this—whether the program increases construction and homebuying—as an open question. That uncertainty is the heart of the trade-off.
Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].
The assistance is tied to newly built homes and paired with a builder option, so the design at least aims at expanding supply rather than only subsidizing demand [1, Sec. 51515.02].
The program lowers the down-payment barrier, the largest single obstacle for many first-time buyers, by covering up to 17 percent of the price [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)].
It carries real consumer protections. The loans must be fixed-rate, origination fees are capped, prepayment penalties are barred, and lenders face agency-set consumer rules [1, Sec. 51515.04].
The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?
If the loan pool underperforms, who actually bears the loss, and could the state face pressure to step in despite the no-liability language?
Does a ceiling of 200 percent of the area median income target the households with the greatest need or does it spread the subsidy to higher earners in costly counties?
How much of the subsidy reaches buyers as lower costs, and how much is captured by builders and sellers through higher new-home prices?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
This measure promises help for middle-class buyers at no cost to taxpayers. That is true only if borrowers repay $25 billion in bonds in full. Ask who is left holding the loss if they do not and whether a state agency running a program this large could really stand aside.
A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a new home only improves affordability if it also gets more homes built. Ask whether this measure will add enough new supply to keep from simply bidding up the price of the homes it covers.

Proposition 37
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
State Revenue Bonds . Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
Proposal
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the "middle-class homeownership loan." Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners' monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program's administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middle-class homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a "qualified builder option." Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
Fiscal Effects
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37's scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
No direct state or local costs.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs.

Proposition 37
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
State Revenue Bonds . Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
Proposal
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the "middle-class homeownership loan." Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners' monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program's administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middle-class homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a "qualified builder option." Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
Fiscal Effects
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37's scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.

Proposition 37
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
State Revenue Bonds . Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
Proposal
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the "middle-class homeownership loan." Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners' monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program's administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middle-class homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a "qualified builder option." Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
Fiscal Effects
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37's scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners' payments on their home loans.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
No direct state or local costs.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)

In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique (https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/determining-the-price-impact-of-harris-down-payment-assistance-proposal/) of down payment assistance programs.
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf) commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026) highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure.
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans.
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7% (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/business/interest-rates-economy-markets-inflation-mortgages.html). Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber).
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.
But Hertzberg said he has a plan.
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards (https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/cra_about.htm).
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion (https://players.brightcove.net/876630612001/2eCBwdutJ_default/index.html?videoId=6406972609112), Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited.
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.
For the record: This story was corrected to note that Prop. 37 loans could be used to purchase any home sold under the policy’s specified price cap, even if the builder is not part of the “qualified builder” program.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.
