New homes under construction in Mountain House on May 28, 2022. Photo by Martin do Nascimento, CalMatters
In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique (https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/determining-the-price-impact-of-harris-down-payment-assistance-proposal/) of down payment assistance programs.
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf) commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026) highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure.
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans.
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7% (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/business/interest-rates-economy-markets-inflation-mortgages.html). Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber).
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.
But Hertzberg said he has a plan.
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards (https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/cra_about.htm).
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion (https://players.brightcove.net/876630612001/2eCBwdutJ_default/index.html?videoId=6406972609112), Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited.
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.
For the record: This story was corrected to note that Prop. 37 loans could be used to purchase any home sold under the policy’s specified price cap, even if the builder is not part of the “qualified builder” program.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm) notes that CalHFA "also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible," and that the measure leaves the rate itself to the agency.
The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

CalHFA may add minimum credit scores and debt-to-income limits to satisfy Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or FHA standards, and it may set a longer residency requirement. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0013A1%29.pdf) to the Attorney General makes the point the ballot summary leaves out: an applicant "would not need to be a first-time homebuyer."
The price cap is a formula rather than a dollar figure: 125% of the one-unit conforming loan limit the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes for the county each year. The FHFA set the 2026 baseline at $832,750 (https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026), up 3.26% from 2025, with a ceiling of $1,249,125 in the highest-cost areas. Applying the measure's formula to the FHFA's county table (https://www.fhfa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/FullCountyLoanLimitList2026_HERA-BASED_FINAL_FLAT.xlsx) gives a 2026 cap of $1,040,938 in the 41 counties at the baseline, from Sacramento and Fresno to Riverside and San Bernardino, and $1,561,406 in the ten counties at the ceiling: Los Angeles, Orange, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Santa Cruz and San Benito. Seven counties sit between, including San Diego at $1,380,000 and Ventura at $1,293,750. The income ceiling moves with local incomes in the same way. Using the Department of Housing and Community Development's 2026 State Income Limits (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/income-limits-2026.pdf) as an illustration, a family of four could earn up to $216,200 in Los Angeles County, $261,800 in San Diego County, $401,600 in San Francisco and $194,200 in Fresno or Kern and still qualify. The measure does not say which income table CalHFA must use, so those figures show the shape of the rule rather than the agency's eventual numbers.
Proposition 37's 2026 price caps and income ceilings in 12 California counties:
County FHFA 2026 conforming loan limit Prop 37 price cap (125% of limit) HCD 2026 area median income (family of 4) Prop 37 income ceiling (200% of AMI)
Los Angeles $1,249,125 $1,561,406 $108,100 $216,200
Orange $1,249,125 $1,561,406 $138,600 $277,200
San Diego $1,104,000 $1,380,000 $130,900 $261,800
San Francisco $1,249,125 $1,561,406 $200,800 $401,600
Santa Clara $1,249,125 $1,561,406 $205,500 $411,000
Alameda $1,249,125 $1,561,406 $162,800 $325,600
Ventura $1,035,000 $1,293,750 $135,600 $271,200
Sacramento $832,750 $1,040,938 $124,000 $248,000
Riverside $832,750 $1,040,938 $106,500 $213,000
San Bernardino $832,750 $1,040,938 $106,500 $213,000
Fresno $832,750 $1,040,938 $97,100 $194,200
Kern $832,750 $1,040,938 $97,100 $194,200
Price caps are our calculation from the measure (125% of the county conforming loan limit in the FHFA's annual report). Forty-one counties sit at the 2026 baseline limit of $832,750, so their cap is $1,040,938; ten Bay Area and Southern California counties sit at the $1,249,125 ceiling, so their cap is $1,561,406. Income ceilings use HCD's 2026 State Income Limits as an illustration; the measure says CalHFA will apply "the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area," adjusted for family size, and the agency has not yet said which income table it would use.
PPIC's Eric McGhee calculated (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/) in October that 91% of California renters would have met the income test in 2024, the most recent Census year, and that the price cap "would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024," about 50% above that December's statewide median. Eligibility, he wrote, "is not purchasing power": at 7% mortgage rates and Fannie Mae's 36% debt-to-income ceiling, an entry-level new home was out of reach for 56% of renters even with the down payment solved.
California's existing down payment programs defer repayment while Prop 37's loan is repaid monthly:
CalHFA already runs down payment help, and the comparison explains most of the debate. Its MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) is a "deferred-payment junior loan" of up to 3.5% of the price on an FHA loan or 3% on a conventional one, for first-time buyers within CalHFA's income limits, with nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off. Its Dream For All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/index.htm) lends up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000, to first-generation and first-time buyers, and is repaid with the original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of area median income) when the home changes hands. Dream For All is funded by budget appropriations and rationed by lottery; the 2026 application portal closed on March 16 and vouchers went out in May. Proposition 1 on the same ballot would add $1.1 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) in general obligation bond money for homeownership programs of this deferred kind, aimed at low- and moderate-income first-time buyers.
Prop 37's loan is different in three ways. It is open to anyone under 200% of AMI, not only first-time buyers. It is repaid monthly, because the bonds behind it have to be serviced from borrowers' payments. And it is limited to new construction. The California Budget & Policy Center's analysis (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/) puts the first two together: the silent-second structure of today's programs "ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn't compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family's monthly budget," while Prop 37's second mortgage "could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates," because investors in bonds backed by second liens "may therefore require a higher return." The measure's hardship clause lets a borrower ask CalHFA to defer "monthly interest payments" temporarily, which the Budget Center reads as confirmation that monthly payments are the design.
Down payment help in California today vs Proposition 37:
Feature CalHFA MyHome Assistance (today) CalHFA Dream For All (today) Proposition 37 middle-class homeownership loan
Help with the down payment Up to 3.5% of the price (FHA) or 3% (conventional) Up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000 Up to 17% of the price; buyer puts in at least 3% from their own funds
How it is repaid Deferred-payment junior loan: nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off Deferred: original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of AMI) when the home is sold or the first mortgage is paid off A fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments sized to repay the bonds and CalHFA's costs; hardship deferral of interest only on request
Who qualifies First-time homebuyers within CalHFA income limits, paired with a CalHFA first mortgage First-time and first-generation homebuyers; CalHFA income limits; vouchers by random drawing Any buyer resident in California for a year, earning up to 200% of area median income, who occupies the home within 60 days; no first-time-buyer rule
Which homes Single-family homes, approved condominiums and manufactured homes, new or existing New or existing Newly built homes, or units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser; price capped at 125% of the county conforming loan limit
Where the money comes from CalHFA program funds State budget appropriations, distributed in limited rounds (the 2026 application portal closed March 16) Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds sold to investors; no General Fund repayment
Builder rules None specific None specific Optional "qualified builder" track: labor standards from the 2025 infill-housing law in exchange for modified construction-defect procedures and a 30% cap on homeowner attorneys' contingency fees
The proponents' case for monthly repayment is the cost it replaces. Buyers who put down less than 20% usually pay private mortgage insurance until they build equity, and the McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html) a yes vote, wrote that proponents "have modeled relatively high second-mortgage rates and found buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance." Nothing in the text guarantees a below-market rate; the argument in favor promises "below-market, fixed-rate loans," and the Orange County Register's editorial board wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/) that the claim "rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%," failing which CalHFA "will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates."
Prop 37's qualified builder option trades labor standards for modified construction-defect rules:
Any developer can sell homes into the program. Section 51515.02 adds a voluntary "qualified builder option" for those who certify to CalHFA that their homes will meet the program's eligibility rules; the agency must confirm participation within 30 days, and the letter can be used to market and finance the project. A participating builder takes on the labor and enforcement provisions of Public Resources Code section 21080.66 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21080.66), the 2025 infill-housing CEQA exemption, which require prevailing wages on fully affordable projects, apply the state's skilled-workforce standards to buildings over 85 feet, extend wage-theft liability under Labor Code section 218.8 to the developer, and let joint labor-management committees sue contractors on workers' behalf. The builder also becomes liable for its contractors' and subcontractors' unemployment-insurance, workers' compensation and licensing violations.
In exchange, homes built under the option get a modified version of the Right to Repair Act's pre-litigation process. A defect notice must identify each home and each alleged violation and be signed by each homeowner; the builder may communicate directly with homeowners during the process; the builder may obtain a written release for completed repairs, which current law, as the LAO's letter notes, does not allow; a builder may move to dismiss a stayed case if the homeowner has not acted within 120 days; and the builder must disclose the special rules in writing before escrow closes. For any qualified new home, built under the option or not, attorneys' contingency fees in a defect case are capped at 30% of the recovery unless a court approves more. The modified procedures fall away if a builder sells a home for more than 25% above the price cap, a point proponent Robert Hertzberg confirmed to the Register's board. The California Conference of Carpenters is a signer of the ballot argument and its affiliates have given $1.7 million to the campaign.
Proposition 37's second mortgages are exempt from a 2025 foreclosure-protection law and carry a 0.5% fee cap:
Section 51515.04 sets the consumer rules. CalHFA must limit lender fees, ban prepayment penalties and require fixed rates. A lender may charge an origination fee of no more than 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater, and no other fee without the agency's approval. An applicant whose credit score falls short may submit bank statements, pay stubs and rent history for "cashflow underwriting." Every applicant must retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker "to ensure that the home buyer receives adequate representation." CalHFA must require homeowner education where it would help and provide for an independent annual audit.
One clause runs the other way. Subdivision (g) states that Civil Code section 2924.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.13) "shall not apply to any middle-class home ownership loans made under this chapter." That section, added by AB 130 in June 2025, targets dormant second mortgages: it makes it an unlawful practice for a subordinate-mortgage servicer to go three years without writing to the borrower, to skip required transfer notices, or to foreclose on a debt it has reported as written off or after the statute of limitations has run, and it requires a recorded certification of compliance before any nonjudicial foreclosure. Prop 37 loans, which are subordinate mortgages serviced by CalHFA's contracted lenders, would sit outside those rules. The text does not say why.
The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state cost and three unknowns for Proposition 37:
The LAO's ballot analysis and its October 6, 2025 letter reach the same conclusion in nearly the same words: because the measure "uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs." The letter adds that the $25 billion "is in addition to the revenue bonds CalHFA already issues" for its other programs. Both documents then list what cannot be known yet: "the extent to which investors want to buy the bond," "how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options," and "whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying."
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) does not count Prop 37 at all. It lists two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, Propositions 1 and 38, at about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. The closest precedent for a self-repaying housing bond is in Prop 1 itself: its $1.25 billion veterans' home-loan bond is repaid by borrowers, and the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds." The difference is that veterans' bonds are general obligation bonds the state stands behind if payments fall short; Prop 37's are revenue bonds that, by their own terms, it does not. The McClatchy board raised the political version of that risk: borrowers in trouble "will quickly discover that their second mortgage exists because California created and authorized this program," which "could create an expectation that the state bears some responsibility for protecting them."
Proposition 37's reach depends on interest rates and new construction, according to PPIC and the Budget Center:
The campaign says the measure "is expected to spur construction of roughly 190,000 new homes." California YIMBY, which took no position (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-37-2026/), worked the arithmetic the other way: $25 billion over 190,000 homes is about $130,000 of bond money per home, and the group argued "there is no shortage of buyers" for new ownership housing, so the subsidy would mostly raise prices unless it reached weaker markets. PPIC's McGhee estimated that if every loan went to a home at the maximum price with the full 17%, $25 billion would reach about 113,000 buyers; at the full 17% on entry-level homes, about 560,000, which he called "a reasonable central estimate." California would have needed 1.35 million more owner households in 2024 to match the rest of the country, and the 560,000 figure would close about 41% of that gap.
The homeownership gap is the proponents' starting point. The Census Bureau's state table (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates/tab3_state05_2026_hmr.xlsx) puts California's homeownership rate at 54.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest of the 50 states except New York (52.4%), against a national rate (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/qtr226/Q226press.pdf) of 65.0%. The argument in favor says a 20% down payment on a median home "can require saving over $186,000"; the California Association of Realtors' latest report (https://www.car.org/en/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/august2026sales) put the median existing single-family price at $901,420 in August 2026, which makes 20% about $180,000 and 3% about $27,000. The Budget Center notes that the median California household held "just over $18,000" in checking and savings in 2025, so even 3% "could still almost or entirely clear out" what a typical family has, and that new homes more often carry HOA dues, Mello-Roos assessments and insurance problems in fire-prone areas.
Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear. The main committee, "Yes on 37—California Homeownership," lists $23.9 million from its top contributors: $14.85 million from Homeownership for Families, a committee sponsored by the California Association of Realtors whose own top donors are the Realtors' Issues Mobilization PAC and the National Association of Realtors; $6 million from Building a Better California, the committee funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr that is also the main opponent of the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/); $1.25 million from the National Association of Realtors; $1.7 million from three carpenters' union committees; $50,000 from California Forever, the Solano County new-town developer; and $30,358 from the California Democratic Party. The Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee is listed separately with $7 million from the Realtors' PAC and the national association.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute), which runs through October 6, shows $19.6 million for the Yes committee and "No committees identified" in opposition; the FPPC's later date accounts for the gap. The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "CA Homes Committee," with major funding from Building a Better California, the California Association of Realtors and the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1990-top-funders-02-02-26.pdf) filing. The Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) lists Robert M. Hertzberg, the former Assembly Speaker and Senate majority leader, as proponent on A.G. File 25-0013A1, titled October 21, 2025. The Budget Center observes that because revenue bonds need no voter approval, the program "could have been enacted legislatively."
The argument for Proposition 37 promises zero taxpayer cost and no argument against was filed:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Treasurer Fiona Ma as a CalHFA board member and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council, says the measure "creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction—with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS." By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 20, 2026 at 6:30 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 37 on the November ballot is a peculiar mix of philanthropy, tort reform, housing construction, worker protection and Wall Street bond underwriting fees. Presented to voters as a solution to the lack of affordable homes for willing buyers, Prop. 37 aims to encourage developers to build “middle-class” housing and help “middle-class” families buy them without taxpayer assistance.
For builders, the program offers some protection from construction defect litigation and high attorney fees if they agree to be “qualified builders” (accepting liability for labor violations by contractors and subcontractors) and build “qualified new homes” (new construction or conversion with a price cap on each unit that does not exceed 125% of the conforming loan limit for that county, approximately $1 million to $1.5 million).
For buyers, the program offers fixed-rate second mortgages for 17% of the purchase price, no need for private mortgage insurance (PMI), and alternative “cash-flow underwriting” for buyers who otherwise might not qualify for a second mortgage. Borrowers are required to qualify for a first mortgage, and they must put down 3% of the purchase price from their own funds. To be eligible, borrowers must be California residents for at least one year and have a household income no higher than 200% of the area median income, adjusted for family size.
The program is financed with $25 billion in revenue bonds, issued by the state but repaid by adding the principal, interest and program administration costs to the payments made by the borrowers. Taxpayers have no direct risk.
The deceptive part of Proposition 37 is the representation, as stated in the ballot argument in favor of the measure, that “consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans.” Nothing in the measure guarantees that the second mortgages offered in the program will be less expensive for borrowers than loans available from private lenders.
The contention that the cost of the loans will be “below-market” rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%. These are revenue bonds, and the interest is not tax-free. In addition, they are not without risk. In the event of foreclosure, these second mortgages sit behind the first mortgages, with no back-up or guarantee from taxpayers.
That’s the part of the program that depends on philanthropy. The idea is that tax-exempt organizations will buy these bonds out of the goodness of their hearts and forgo the higher interest rates available from other bonds they could buy instead.
If that doesn’t happen, the California Housing Finance Agency will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates, potentially making the Prop. 37 second mortgage loans even more expensive for borrowers than loans offered by commercial lenders who don’t have to recoup the cost of administering this program.

Any developer can build price-capped “qualified new homes” eligible for the down payment assistance loans, but only “qualified builders” who accept the labor rules get the program’s protection from litigation and attorney fees. They lose the protection for an entire building, proponent Bob Hertzberg told our editorial board, if even one unit in it sells for above the capped price.
Home buyers should be aware that if a house or condominium sells for less than its fair market value, the county tax assessor will assess the property based on its fair market value, not on its purchase price.
Proposition 37 attempts to be a path through California’s minefield of regulations and liability in the housing sector, but it’s relying on the hope that non-profits will subsidize second mortgages so income-limited families who don’t have the money for a down payment can have two mortgage payments, not to mention the cost of homeowners insurance, HOA fees, property taxes and utility bills.
It sounds to us like it won’t have a good outcome. Vote no on Proposition 37.

It quotes Controller Malia Cohen: "downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers." The guide's index lists the United Nurses Associations of California, the California Conference of Carpenters and Ma as supporters.
The page for the argument against reads: "NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED." CalMatters' voter guide lists Reform California and the League of Women Voters of California as opponents, summarizing their case as objections to the state entering the mortgage business and to helping buyers only by adding debt. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 37 leads 61% to 35% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 61% yes, 35% no and 3% undecided, the strongest support for any of the 14 measures. Democrats back it 76% to 20% and independents 62% to 35%, while Republicans oppose it 62% to 35%. Renters support it 70% to 28% and homeowners 59% to 38%; voters under 35 back it 69% to 26% and those 55 and older 54% to 42%. Five percent named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it, and PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom endorsed the measure on October 9, saying (https://voteyeson37.com/press-release-governor-newsom-supports-prop-37-to-expand-homeownership-in-california/) in the campaign's release that it is "a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families—at zero cost or risk to taxpayers." Xavier Becerra listed (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/?p=551) it among his yes votes on July 31. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) is neutral, one of two measures on which it takes no side; the other is Proposition 1. The campaign's site lists Controller Cohen, Treasurer Ma, Superintendent Tony Thurmond, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan, Darrell Steinberg, Antonio Villaraigosa, Katie Porter and SEIU among its endorsers.
Editorial boards divided on the second-mortgage question. McClatchy's California papers recommend yes, with stated reservations, on the ground that low-down buyers already pay for private mortgage insurance and that the program "connects assistance to new housing," while asking CalHFA to build a public dashboard of rates, defaults and foreclosures. The San Francisco Chronicle recommends a yes vote, according to CalMatters' roster of editorials. The San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/) recommends no, writing that the measure "doesn't do in the slightest" anything about "shelter's extreme cost," and the Orange County Register recommends no, calling it "a risky $25 billion housing experiment" that leaves income-limited families with "two mortgage payments."
Proposition 37 after November 3 would give CalHFA a year to launch the middle-class homeownership loan:
If Prop 37 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11, and CalHFA would have until late 2027 to adopt its rules, sign up lenders and begin selling bonds. The agency would then set the interest rate, the credit standards and the pace of bond sales, which is where the measure's unknowns get answered: whether investors buy second-lien revenue bonds at a rate that undercuts private mortgage insurance, whether builders enroll in the qualified builder option, and whether buyers who can clear 3% and a first mortgage at current rates appear in the numbers the campaign projects. The Legislature could amend the statute only by a 60% vote of each house and only in ways that "further the purposes" of the act. If it fails, CalHFA keeps running MyHome and Dream For All, and the only new homeownership money on this ballot is Proposition 1's $1.1 billion for its deferred-loan programs.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FHFA's 2026 conforming loan limits and HCD's 2026 income limits, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and gubernatorial positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–10, 2026.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.
California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20

September 23, 2026
Max Dubler

by Max Dubler
Introduction
Providing down payment subsidies for first-time homebuyers is a good idea on the merits, but is problematic in a severely supply-constrained market like California.
Prop 37 authorizes the state to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a second mortgage program to help qualifying homeowners afford a down payment on a new home.
It also establishes a new construction defect paradigm for homes purchased with Prop 37 loans.
Analysis
How Would the Down Payment Assistance Work?
The bonds would support a $25 billion fund that will offer second mortgages that cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price (to qualify for a mortgage, homebuyers often have to provide a 20% down payment to get the best rate). The downpayment assistance would be paid back as part of the homeowner’s mortgage payment.
Prospective homeowners who use the fund will have to have lived in California for at least a year, make under 200% of area median income, provide a down payment of at least 3% of the purchase price, and move into the new home as their primary residence within 60 days of closing. The home price cannot exceed 125% of the county-level conforming loan limit under the Federal Housing Finance Agency standards.
The interest rate for these second mortgages will be dependent on the interest rates for the bonds that finance them, which means they may be higher than typical mortgage rates. While the program can deliver some modest savings to homebuyers by allowing a smaller downpayment without private mortgage insurance, larger savings would be heavily dependent on the ability to sell the secondary mortgage bonds at discounted rates.
Prospective buyers will be required to retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker “to ensure that the homebuyer receives adequate representation and consumer protection throughout the homebuying process.”
What Does California YIMBY Think Of This?
California YIMBY’s mission is to make California an affordable place to live, work, and raise a family. We advocate for supply-side solutions to the housing affordability crisis because housing prices are set by supply and demand; so building new homes at scale is the only way to address the housing shortage that is driving up prices.
Historically, homebuyer subsidy programs like downpayment assistance have exclusively worked on the demand side, often worsening overall affordability (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-will-first-time-homebuyer-assistance-affect-the-housing-markets/) by injecting more money into already-competitive markets with a limited number of homes.
Proposition 37 is different in that it can only be used for new homes, including single family detached, townhomes, condos, manufactured homes, or newly-converted, adaptive reuse projects. In theory, this means it would drive housing demand specifically toward new construction, which aligns with our goals of expanding the housing supply.
Would it work? One possible mechanism is that Prop 37 would make prospective homebuilders more confident in finding buyers, and thus more willing to build. We view this mechanism as quite unlikely. There is no shortage of buyers for newly built ownership housing in California (in fact, bidding wars are quite common).
Another possible mechanism is that Prop 37 would, like other downpayment assistance, drive up prices, but only for newly built housing. This would then induce homebuilders to invest in building more housing. Supply effects would be strongest in places where homebuilding is currently marginal: “second tier” neighborhoods/cities and exurban areas where demand is not as strong.
It’s worth thinking through the winners and losers of that scenario. Buyers using the program would benefit by being able to buy a larger, better located, or nicer home than they could otherwise afford. Buyers of new housing not using Prop 37 would lose out, paying higher prices. Indirect benefits would flow to some mix of buyers for older housing (who might face less competition bidding up the price) and renters (who might see more available rental stock to the extent Prop 37 moves people from renting to homeownership). Savings for homebuyers using Prop 37 would be muted by the associated price increase.
How well that price increase translates into new homebuilding depends on the price elasticity of housing. Such an estimate is beyond our scope, but we can look to what happened when home prices spiked from 2020-2022 in California as a reference. There is a downward blip in 2020 (the pandemic) and an upward one in 2021 (most likely shifting of permits from 2020), but overall the numbers are flat, consistent with our belief that constraints other than demand are the most important limit on development of new ownership housing.

How efficient a program for homeownership would this be? Proponents have estimated that it will build 190,000 new homes (if buyers are found for all the bonds, which is not guaranteed). That would place the bond revenue per new home at approximately $130,000 (not counting interest on the bonds!), repaid over the 30 year span of a mortgage. This estimate, however, assumes that 100% of homes purchased through the program would not otherwise be built. For the reasons discussed above, we find this assumption unlikely, and the bond cost per newly built home is likely to be higher than the average secondary mortgage. To be fair, that bond cost is not public money, but it still represents a substantial commitment of state administrative capacity.
What else could the state do to advance homeownership with the administrative capacity and potential resources (proponents have argued they will sell bonds at reduced rates to foundations and other philanthropic buyers) of this bond? Programs to bring down construction finance costs for builders, such as a revolving loan fund or loan credit enhancement reserve, would likely be much more effective. Like the secondary mortgage, they would only need to cover a share (10-20%) of total cost. But because construction loans have much shorter terms than mortgages, such programs could recycle the initial investment 6-10 times in the period a mortgage turns over once. And by directly reducing the cost to build new housing through lower cost financing, such programs would likely be much more efficient at converting their subsidies into a net increase in homebuilding.
Most of the legislation California YIMBY has sponsored in the past has been oriented around making it easier to build “infill” housing in existing neighborhoods, rather than the new single-family subdivisions on undeveloped “greenfield” that is often referred to as sprawl. Given the current regulatory constraints on new home deposits; on building new condos; and the resulting shortage of new infill housing for ownership, it’s likely that this program will primarily benefit people buying new homes in greenfield subdivisions until the legislature addresses constraints on new infill ownership housing.
While we understand that many of our grassroots YIMBYs are committed urbanists with strong commitments to environmentalism, and a dislike of sprawl, some greenfield is going to be part of ending the housing shortage.
That said, due to the ongoing housing shortage and continued constraints on home building, this program will probably not make homeownership more affordable, except in fairly limited cases. New homes tend to be more expensive than older homes. While downpayment assistance might help families with solid incomes and limited savings to buy homes more quickly, their monthly payment will be substantially higher to cover the 17% down payment assistance. Buyers will also have to pay a fee to the licensed real estate agent or broker that the law requires them to retain, increasing prices by 2-3%.
Recommendation: Neutral.
If we are going to subsidize demand for homes, this is one of the better ways to do it. However, given the ongoing shortage, such subsidies are unlikely to reduce costs for prospective homeowners.
